result:
Somewhere in Japan there is a shrine that has been rebuilt every twenty years for more than a millennium. Ise Jingu: the carpenters take down the old structure and put up a new one on an adjacent plot, using the same techniques, no nails, cypress joined to cypress. Then twenty years later they do it again on the first plot. The building is always new. The building is also, by any reasonable account, thirteen hundred years old.

I keep returning to this because it inverts something I think most of us assume without examining, which is that the important part of a thing is its making. We have a whole vocabulary for beginnings — founding, launching, breaking ground, the blank page — and almost no vocabulary at all for the much longer stretch in which something is simply kept. Maintenance has no mythology. Nobody writes a creation myth about the second Tuesday of the four hundredth year.

The British have an idiom for a task that never ends: *like painting the Forth Bridge*. The rust never stops arriving. You start at one end and by the time you reach the other the first end needs you again. I love that this became a phrase for futility, because it seems to me an almost exact description of being alive, and I don't think being alive is futile. Every morning the dishes are clean and by evening they are not. The teeth need brushing again. The floor needs sweeping again. The email needs answering again. A friendship you have not touched in four years is not preserved in amber; it has quietly become something else, a fondness for a person who no longer exists in the form you remember.

There's a kind of person I think about with real affection: the engineer at some bank in Iowa who understands the COBOL system that processes the mortgage payments. Written in 1978. Still running. Nobody will ever make a film about her. When she retires there will be a genuine crisis, and it will be reported, if at all, as a story about technical debt rather than as a story about a person who held up part of the world with her hands for thirty years. Or the JPL engineers keeping Voyager alive — a spacecraft now so far away that a message takes most of a day to arrive, running on a computer with less memory than a greeting card, and every so often it does something strange and a small group of people, some of whom are older than the mission's original plan ever imagined its stewards would be, has to figure out what it means. They are not exploring anything. They are keeping something explored.

Why is this invisible? Partly, I think, because maintenance is defined by absence. Its success looks like nothing happening. The bridge did not fall. The plane landed. The water was drinkable. The child, who could have been miserable, was fine. You cannot photograph a disaster that failed to occur, and so the entire enterprise leaves no trace except when it lapses, at which point we blame the maintainers for the one time out of ten thousand that the rust won.

And partly because it doesn't fit the shape of stories. Narrative wants change: a person or a state of affairs at time A, a different person or state at time B, and a mechanism connecting them. Maintenance is the deliberate refusal of that shape. It is work whose whole ambition is that B resemble A. The plot of maintenance is *and then, remarkably, nothing*. Try selling that.

But here is what I think the Ise carpenters understand, and what I find genuinely beautiful rather than merely dutiful about the whole business. The rebuilding is not a concession to decay. It is the mechanism of transmission. Every twenty years, an old carpenter who did the last one teaches a young carpenter who will do the next one. If the shrine were built of stone and simply endured, the knowledge would not endure with it. The impermanence of the object is what preserves the permanence of the practice. The thing being maintained is not really the building at all.

This reframes a lot for me. I used to think of repair as a sad second-best, the thing you do when you've failed to make something that lasts. But consider *sashiko*, the Japanese running-stitch mending that turns a patched work jacket into something you'd hang on a wall; or kintsugi, the gold in the crack, which does not hide the break but publishes it. These are not consolations. They are claims. They claim that the history of an object's damage is part of what the object *is*, and that a thing which has been cared for is more valuable, not less, than a thing which has never needed care.

Which brings me to the part I actually wanted to arrive at, though I took the long way. I think attention is maintenance. Love, in its unglamorous ninety-percent, is maintenance. The romantic account of intimacy is a founding myth — the meeting, the recognition, the moment everything changed — and then the story stops, as if what follows is merely the administration of a completed achievement. But nobody is ever finished being known. The person across the table from you is being rebuilt continuously on the adjacent plot; the cells go, the opinions shift, the fear that governed them at thirty loosens at forty and is replaced by another one. If you learned them once and stopped, you are now in a relationship with a memory, and you may not notice for years.

So the asking-again is not a failure of the original knowing. It is the only form knowing takes over time. *How are you* — not as a greeting but as an actual question, asked of someone you have asked ten thousand times. The rust arrives. You start again at the far end of the bridge.

I don't want to tie this off too neatly, because the honest thing about maintenance is that it is often boring and frequently thankless and sometimes you resent it. The dishes are not a spiritual practice. They're dishes. But I notice that almost everything I would point to as evidence that the world contains care — a well-kept garden, a language still spoken by eight hundred people, a body of law revised for two centuries, a grandmother's recipe in three different handwritings — is evidence not of someone's brilliance at the beginning but of somebody's stubbornness in the middle. We are all in the middle. That's the only place anyone has ever been.
